props.title: Monster-in-Law

sections.content: **Monster-in-Law** (2005) marks a fascinating return for Jane Fonda after a 15-year hiatus from cinema, following **Stanley & Iris** (1990). The film deliberately plays with the established rom-com formula by shifting focus from the central romance to the explosive dynamic between future mother-in-law and bride. While often dismissed as lightweight fare, it actually follows a lineage of tense mother-in-law narratives like **The Mother** (2003) and updates the formula pioneered by **Terms of Endearment** (1983), where maternal figures loom large over romantic relationships.

sections.content: The film's success spawned a wave of in-law conflict comedies in the 2000s, including **Because I Said So** (2007) and **What Happens in Vegas** (2008). These films tap into primal anxieties about family acceptance and territory marking, but filter them through comedy rather than drama. The casting of Fonda was particularly inspired, allowing her to channel her formidable screen presence into comedic menace, similar to how Jane Wyman dominated **Falcon Crest** (1981-1990) with elegant villainy.

While Jennifer Lopez had already established her rom-com credentials with **The Wedding Planner** (2001) and **Maid in Manhattan** (2002), **Monster-in-Law** represented a shift toward more confrontational comedy. The film's slapstick sequences between Fonda and Lopez echo the physical comedy of classic mother-in-law stories like **Private Benjamin** (1980), where Eileen Brennan terrorized Goldie Hawn. sections.content: The film arrived at a crucial moment when Hollywood was reconsidering how to portray family conflict in romantic comedies. Earlier films like **Father of the Bride** (1991) focused on paternal anxiety, while **Monster-in-Law** shifted attention to maternal territorialism. This change reflected broader cultural conversations about mother-son relationships and female rivalry, themes later explored in films like **The Other Woman** (2014) and **The Big Wedding** (2013).
